Growing degree-days from daily minimum and maximum temperatures

Source: R/degree_days.R
degree_days.Rd

Computes daily growing degree-days (GDD, in degree Celsius day) with the averaging, single sine, single triangle, double sine or double triangle methods, optionally bounded by an upper developmental threshold.

Usage

degree_days(
  tmin,
  tmax,
  method = c("single_sine", "average", "single_triangle", "double_sine",
    "double_triangle"),
  base = 10,
  upper = NULL,
  cutoff = c("horizontal", "vertical", "intermediate"),
  tmin_next = NULL
)

Arguments

tmin, tmax

Numeric vectors of daily minimum and maximum temperatures (degrees Celsius), of equal length, ordered in time for double methods.

method

One of "single_sine" (default), "average", "single_triangle", "double_sine" or "double_triangle".

base

Lower developmental threshold (degrees Celsius).

upper

Optional upper developmental threshold (degrees Celsius).

cutoff

Upper threshold treatment: "horizontal" (default), "vertical" or "intermediate". Ignored when upper is NULL.

tmin_next

Optional numeric vector with the minimum temperature of the following day, used only by double methods.

Value

Numeric vector of daily degree-days (degree Celsius day), same length as tmin.

Methods

All sine and triangle methods are evaluated with closed-form expressions; no hourly temperatures are generated.

  • "average": \(\max(0, (T_{max} + T_{min}) / 2 - T_b)\) (McMaster & Wilhelm 1997, method 1). With an upper threshold the cutoff is applied to the daily mean.

  • "single_sine": a sine wave between tmin and tmax over 24 h (Baskerville & Emin 1969).

  • "single_triangle": a symmetric triangle between tmin and tmax (Lindsey & Newman 1956; Sevacherian et al. 1977).

  • "double_sine", "double_triangle": the day is split into two half-day segments: tmin to tmax of the same day, then tmax to the minimum of the following day (tmin_next). Each half contributes half a day (Allen 1976; Zalom et al. 1983).

Upper threshold cutoffs

With an upper threshold \(T_u\):

  • "horizontal": development continues at the constant rate reached at \(T_u\); the area above \(T_u\) is removed.

  • "vertical": no development while temperature exceeds \(T_u\); the whole area under the curve during those hours is removed.

  • "intermediate": development decreases linearly above \(T_u\) with slope -1 (the area above \(T_u\) is subtracted a second time), with the rate floored at zero. The floor only matters when temperatures exceed \(2T_u - T_b\).

The three cutoffs coincide when temperatures stay below upper and give different results otherwise; they are not interchangeable.

Missing values and boundaries

Missing tmin or tmax give NA for that day. Double methods need the minimum of the next day; when tmin_next is NULL it is taken from the following element of tmin, and the last day is NA. Supply tmin_next explicitly to close the series (for a cyclic climatological year pass c(tmin[-1], tmin[1])). If the following minimum is above the current maximum, the second half-day segment is evaluated between the two values in increasing order.

References

Allen, J. C. (1976). A modified sine wave method for calculating degree days. Environmental Entomology, 5(3), 388-396.

Baskerville, G. L., & Emin, P. (1969). Rapid estimation of heat accumulation from maximum and minimum temperatures. Ecology, 50(3), 514-517.

Lindsey, A. A., & Newman, J. E. (1956). Use of official weather data in spring time temperature analysis of an Indiana phenological record. Ecology, 37(4), 812-823.

McMaster, G. S., & Wilhelm, W. W. (1997). Growing degree-days: one equation, two interpretations. Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, 87(4), 291-300.

Sevacherian, V., Stern, V. M., & Mueller, A. J. (1977). Heat accumulation for timing Lygus control measures in a safflower-cotton complex. Journal of Economic Entomology, 70(4), 399-402.

Zalom, F. G., Goodell, P. B., Wilson, L. T., Barnett, W. W., & Bentley, W. J. (1983). Degree-days: the calculation and use of heat units in pest management. University of California DANR Leaflet 21373.

See also

degree_hours() for hourly temperatures.

Examples

tmin <- c(4, 8, 12, 15)
tmax <- c(16, 22, 28, 34)
degree_days(tmin, tmax, method = "average", base = 10)
#> [1]  0.0  5.0 10.0 14.5
degree_days(tmin, tmax, method = "single_sine", base = 10)
#> [1]  1.909859  5.325635 10.000000 14.500000
degree_days(tmin, tmax, method = "single_sine", base = 10, upper = 30,
            cutoff = "vertical")
#> [1]  1.909859  5.325635 10.000000  7.634159
degree_days(tmin, tmax, method = "double_sine", base = 10,
            tmin_next = c(tmin[-1], 10))
#> [1]  2.172925  6.162818 10.750000 13.250000
